claims.text: Tungsten-based high-entropy alloys can serve as intermediate transition layers in plasma-facing reactor components.
Tungsten-based refractory HEAs may contain Mo, Nb, and Ta.
Forging above the recrystallization temperature followed by brief annealing below the solidus will align and coarsen grains.
The proposed forging and annealing treatment will reduce the density of grain boundaries.
A brief near-solidus anneal will retain coherent strengthening precipitates.
The proposed performance should hold at approximately 600–1000 °C under thermal cycling and moderate tensile loading.
Controlled grain growth and orientation will minimize phonon scattering at grain boundaries.
Reduced phonon scattering at grain boundaries will increase the alloy's thermal conductivity.
Coherent precipitates inhibit dislocation motion and strengthen HEAs at high temperature.
Retention of a coherent precipitate network will preserve high-temperature mechanical integrity after forging and annealing.
The treatment will produce a measurable increase in thermal conductivity relative to as-cast or conventionally processed tungsten-based HEAs.
The treatment will maintain or slightly enhance high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to untreated tungsten-based HEAs.
Refractory HEAs containing tungsten exhibit high-temperature strength and fatigue resistance.
Current tungsten-based HEAs have limited thermal conductivity because of fine grains and numerous grain boundaries.
An interlayer is needed between tungsten plasma-facing material and a CuCrZr heat sink because their suitable operating-temperature ranges differ.
Excessive annealing or treatment above the solidus could degrade the coherent precipitate network and reduce strength.
Reactor components are exposed to high temperature, high heat flux, and intense high-energy neutron flux.
Extreme neutron irradiation may alter the treated microstructure in ways not captured by the proposed experiment.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention call for grain coarsening and fewer grain boundaries, whereas the mechanism also attributes mechanical integrity to microstructural refinement. No distinction between refinement of precipitates and refinement of grains is supplied, making these descriptions internally ambiguous.
